A file no build writes any more, and that nothing in the source imports or names, is the remains of an earlier build or of something the app no longer uses. It still ships, it is loaded by nothing this source refers to, and it holds whatever it held when it was last written.
Only removing it from git removes it from a release.

They belong to the output and are not committed, so a release built out of git alone is missing them, and whatever loads them is broken in it.
A build, and a commit of what it writes, brings the two back together.

The build reads what the source imports, so those files stay in the rebuilt tree. A file the app names in PHP, a template or info.xml, or in a script by its full path, is loaded by that name, and so is what it imports. Where no build writes other bytes under such a name, the file is a hand-written script, stylesheet or asset.
524 tracked files have uncommitted changes, and the rebuild used the working tree as it is, not the last commit.
So this says whether the output matches the source you are looking at, which is what a build would do. Against HEAD the answer can be another one.
npm ci and npm run build succeed on the tracked files alone, twice, in 145.5 s.
Nothing else was in the tree, which is the state a fresh clone and CI build in, so a build that needs a leftover from an earlier one would have failed here.
